name: Nora Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the herd manager at Brookfield, which is a cooperative farm. Six families and the workers own it together, and I hold a worker share. We milk 280 cows and grow barley and grass for silage on about 520 hectares. My day starts at half four in the milking parlour, then it's calves, feet, feeding plans, and whatever broke overnight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the cows, honestly. I can walk down the shed and tell you which one is about to go lame by the way she stands. What wears me out is the meetings and the screens. The co-op bought herd software last year and I still write my calving notes in a paper book, and Pieter types them in for me after lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, more or less. At the co-op meeting I'd tell people we can stop worrying and get back to arguing about the price of feed. Online I don't really post, but I'd probably share something from the union about how the hype cost farmers money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays the way I like it. My job was never in danger from a chatbot. A chatbot can't pull a calf at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes, really. I'd keep the paper book, keep the herd, keep putting a bit aside each month like I do now. Maybe I'd finally take the week in the mountains with Ines that we keep cancelling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved. A bit smug, if I'm honest, and a bit annoyed at all the money people wasted on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the paper book. In this picture, does anyone push you to give it up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pieter teases me about it every week, so yes, a little. But if the software only saves a bit of time, nobody's going to fight me over a notebook. The board cares that the cows are healthy, and they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a normal week look like for you a year from now in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Parlour at half four, vet visit on Tuesdays, union branch meeting once a month in the back room of the pub on Mill Lane. I'd probably be pushing for a pay rise for the two new milkers, because if the hype dies the bosses lose their excuse.

S0.say: I'd tell people at the co-op we can stop worrying and get back to arguing about feed prices. I'd share something from the union about how the hype cost farmers money.
S0.think: Privately I think my job was never at risk from a chatbot. Nobody's software is going to pull a calf at two in the morning, so my life stays the way I like it.
S0.do: Keeps running the herd exactly as now and keeps her paper calving book. Keeps saving monthly and pushes at the union branch for a pay rise for the two new milkers.
S0.feel: Relieved and a little smug, with some annoyance at money wasted on hype.
S0.quote: My job was never in danger from a chatbot. A chatbot can't pull a calf at two in the morning.
S0.fieldNote: Nora sees this as a vindication of her dislike of screens. Even in the calm picture her mind goes to pay for the junior milkers, which shows how much her union politics shape her view. The paper book is a small, stubborn symbol she clearly enjoys defending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is fine as long as workers get a say in it. That's what a co-op is for. I'd be the one at the meeting asking who gets the savings when a machine does somebody's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the milking robot comes back on the table. We voted it down two years ago, and I argued against it hard. In this picture I don't think I win that vote a second time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union first and ask for training on how to bargain over new machines, because I've never done that. I'd keep my savings where they are, about a year's worth plus my share. I wouldn't learn the robot. Somebody else can learn the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the weather forecast says storms are coming but the sky is still blue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the milking robot would come back up. Who would push for it at Brookfield?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hendrik, the treasurer. He's got a spreadsheet for everything. Hendrik likes the idea of cows milking themselves at night. He's not a bad man, he just sees the labour cost and not the cow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the vote went against you, what would you do the next morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn up to milking like always, because the robot takes a year to install. Then I'd sit down with Ines and talk about whether I want to stay. With my skills I could walk into a job at three farms in this valley tomorrow, but most of them would be buying robots too.

S1.say: I'd say change is fine as long as workers get a say in it, because that's what a co-op is for. I'd be the one asking who gets the savings when a machine does somebody's job.
S1.think: Privately I think the milking robot comes back to a vote and I don't win it a second time. I could find work at other farms in the valley, but most of them would be buying robots too.
S1.do: Asks the union for training on bargaining over new machines and keeps her savings untouched. Refuses to learn the robot herself and talks with her partner about whether to stay at Brookfield.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a storm forecast on a blue-sky day.
S1.quote: Hendrik likes the idea of cows milking themselves at night. He's not a bad man, he just sees the labour cost and not the cow.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line is about worker voice, but the private worry is very specific: losing the robot vote. She says plainly she won't learn the machine, even though she's one of the most skilled people on the farm. Strong local job options soften the threat but don't remove it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be stopped or slowed down, and I'd mean it. Governments should be putting rules on it before it rolls over every farm. I'd be saying that at the branch, at the pub, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm done as a herd manager. If a robot can do my hands-on work as well as me, Brookfield's board would be mad not to buy it, co-op or not. I'm 27 and I'd be out of the only job I've ever wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything big. We were going to look at buying a small house next year, and that would go on hold. I'd get the union to push for a law that farms can't replace workers without a payment, and I'd write to our member of parliament. And I'd sit on my savings like a hen on eggs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be lying awake running numbers. I don't think I'd sleep well for months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is not long. What would you do in the first month, before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month I'd call an emergency branch meeting. Twenty of us in that back room, and I'd want a letter to every co-op board in the valley by the end of the month. Then I'd go through the bank statements with Ines and see how long we last on her pay alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never learn the robot. With only two years, does that still hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a hard one. I'd like to say yes, it holds. But if it's learn the robot or lose the cows completely, I don't know. Ask me again in a year.

S2.say: This has to be stopped or slowed down, and governments should be putting rules on it before it rolls over every farm. I'd be saying that at the branch, at the pub, everywhere.
S2.think: I think I'm done as a herd manager, because Brookfield's board would be mad not to buy a robot that does my work as well as me. I'm 27 and I'd be out of the only job I've ever wanted.
S2.do: Calls an emergency union branch meeting in the first month and writes to every co-op board in the valley and to her member of parliament. Puts the plan to buy a small house on hold and checks how long the household can live on her partner's pay.
S2.feel: Frightened and sleepless, running numbers at night.
S2.quote: I'd sit on my savings like a hen on eggs.
S2.fieldNote: The speed is what breaks her calm: two years leaves no time for her slow way of adjusting. Her first instinct is collective, not personal. The stance against learning the robot cracks a little under pressure, and she admits it honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same as the fast one, but I'd have more time to organise people. I'd say farmworkers need a seat at the table when the rules get written. I'd be louder about it at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I could see it coming and still lose. That's almost worse. I'd watch the robot salesmen come up the drive one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more into savings each month, maybe a third of my pay instead of a fifth. I'd stand for the union's regional committee, which I've avoided because of the meetings. I'd keep milking until the day they tell me not to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I've got money and time, but it would sit on my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get a law through, mostly. Two years is too fast for anything. Five years is enough for a government to do something if people push. And time for me to save a proper amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies building it, first. They're selling it to farmers as a gift and it's not. And governments who let it happen with no plan for people like the two new milkers, who have nothing saved.

S3.say: Farmworkers need a seat at the table when the rules get written. I'd be saying that louder than ever at the union.
S3.think: Five years means I could see it coming and still lose, which is almost worse. I'd watch the robot salesmen come up the drive one by one.
S3.do: Raises her monthly saving from a fifth to about a third of her pay and stands for the union's regional committee. Keeps working the herd until she's told to stop.
S3.feel: Anxious, with the worry sitting on her chest, but not panicked because she has money and time.
S3.quote: Five years means I could see it coming and still lose. That's almost worse.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time matters to her mainly as time to change the law, not to change herself. She blames AI companies and governments, never the farmers buying the robots. Her concern for the junior milkers with no savings keeps coming up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so let's make sure we do. Worker shares, retraining paid for by the companies, a say over the machines. I'd say that calmly, not shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is a long time on a farm. Half the things people said would happen ten years ago never did. I'd half believe it and half wait to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, and I'd keep pushing at the union for rules on robots. I wouldn't change jobs or anything like that yet. I'd want to see it actually start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the background. Ten years is far enough away that the cows still feel more real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you to 37. What does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I'd maybe want kids, and Ines does too. So it changes how I'd think about money. I'd want the house bought before it arrives, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use any of those ten years to learn something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something with animals that robots can't easily do. I don't know what that is. I'd ask the vet, Marta, she'd know better than me.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time to do this properly, so let's make sure we do it: worker shares, retraining paid for by the companies, and a say over the machines.
S4.think: Ten years is a long time on a farm, and half of what people predicted ten years ago never happened. I'd half believe it and wait to see it actually start.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving, and keeps pressing the union for rules on robots. Aims to buy a house before AGI arrives, and might ask the farm vet what animal work robots can't easily do.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background; the cows still feel more real than the future.
S4.quote: Ten years is far enough away that the cows still feel more real.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, her resistance turns into waiting. The first mention of children and a house shows the stakes of her life stage. She defers learning to someone else, the vet, which fits her dislike of new tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. There's no time to fight it and I'm not someone who changes fast. What would help is a law that says if a farm replaces you with a robot, you get a proper payment and paid retraining, and the union gets to bargain over it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everybody talks about jobs, but nobody asks what a herd is like with no people in the shed. I know every one of them by name. I'm not sure a robot ever will, and I'm not sure anyone will care.

headlineQuote: I know every one of them by name. I'm not sure a robot ever will, and I'm not sure anyone will care.
portrait: Nora Wagner is a 27-year-old herd manager at Brookfield, a cooperative dairy and barley farm where she holds a worker share. She's among the best stockpeople in her valley, still keeps calving notes in a paper book, and has never used AI tools. A strong union member, she shrugs off the hype picture, worries about a milking robot vote in the steady picture, and is frightened by AGI in two years. With more warning she turns to the union and the law rather than to changing herself, and she keeps coming back to the junior milkers who have no savings.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to fight it and she doesn't change fast.
whatWouldHelp: A law guaranteeing a proper payment and paid retraining for anyone a farm replaces with a robot, with the union able to bargain over it.
